prompt: What reaction converts an open-chain monosaccharide into its cyclic form?

choices.text: Intramolecular nucleophilic addition of an –OH group to the carbonyl group, giving a cyclic hemiacetal
Intramolecular dehydration of two –OH groups, giving a cyclic ether
choices.why: No water is lost. The –OH adds to the carbonyl group, and the ring that forms is a hemiacetal.

choices.text: Reaction of the carbonyl group of one sugar with an –OH group of a second sugar molecule
choices.why: Cyclization is intramolecular: the carbonyl and the –OH are in the same molecule.

choices.text: Intramolecular nucleophilic addition of an –OH group to the carbonyl group, giving a cyclic acetal
choices.why: One alcohol adding to a carbonyl gives a hemiacetal, not an acetal. Acetals (glycosides) need a second alcohol.

explanation: Aldehydes and ketones react reversibly with alcohols to form hemiacetals. When the carbonyl and the hydroxyl group are in the same molecule, an intramolecular nucleophilic addition takes place, giving a cyclic hemiacetal.

prompt: Which cyclic hemiacetal ring sizes are relatively strain-free and particularly stable?

choices.text: Five- and six-membered rings
Three- and four-membered rings
choices.why: Small rings are strained. The section names five- and six-membered rings as strain-free.

choices.text: Six-membered rings only
choices.why: Five-membered rings (furanoses) are also relatively strain-free; fructose and ribose form them.

choices.text: Six- and seven-membered rings
choices.why: The section names five- and six-membered rings.

explanation: Five- and six-membered cyclic hemiacetals are relatively strain-free and particularly stable, so many carbohydrates exist in an equilibrium between open-chain and cyclic forms.

prompt: Glucose exists in aqueous solution mainly in a six-membered pyranose form. Which –OH group adds to the carbon 1 carbonyl to form it?

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 5
The –OH at carbon 4
choices.why: Ring closure through the carbon 4 oxygen would give a five-membered ring, not a pyranose.

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 6
choices.why: Glucose's pyranose ring is closed by the carbon 5 –OH; carbon 6 stays outside the ring as –CH2OH. (It is fructose whose pyranose uses the carbon 6 –OH, adding to its carbon 2 carbonyl.)

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 2
choices.why: Carbon 2 is next to the carbonyl; it can't close a six-membered ring.

explanation: Glucose exists in aqueous solution primarily in the six-membered pyranose form resulting from intramolecular nucleophilic addition of the –OH group at carbon 5 to the carbon 1 carbonyl group. The ring holds carbons 1 through 5 and the oxygen from carbon 5.

prompt: Where does the name pyranose come from?

choices.text: Pyran, the name of the unsaturated six-membered cyclic ether
Pyran, the name of the unsaturated five-membered cyclic ether
choices.why: Pyranose rings are six-membered; the five-membered ring form is the furanose.

choices.text: Pyruvate, a three-carbon keto acid anion
choices.why: The name comes from pyran, the six-membered cyclic ether, not from pyruvate.

choices.text: The Greek word for fire, because the ring forms on heating
choices.why: Glucose cyclizes in aqueous solution without heating. The name comes from pyran.

explanation: The name pyranose is derived from pyran, the name of the unsaturated six-membered cyclic ether. A five-membered cyclic hemiacetal form is called a furanose.

prompt: When a D sugar is drawn as a pyranose ring by the usual convention, where does an –OH group that is on the right in the Fischer projection end up?

choices.text: On the bottom face of the ring
On the top face of the ring
choices.why: An –OH on the left in the Fischer projection goes on the top face; one on the right goes on the bottom.

choices.text: Always in an axial position
choices.why: Right or left in the Fischer projection decides top or bottom face, not axial or equatorial.

choices.text: In the ring itself, as the ring oxygen
choices.why: Only the –OH that adds to the carbonyl becomes the ring oxygen (carbon 5's, for glucose).

explanation: With the hemiacetal oxygen drawn at the right rear, an –OH group on the right in a Fischer projection is on the bottom face of the pyranose ring, and an –OH group on the left is on the top face.

prompt: In the pyranose ring of a D sugar, where is the terminal –CH2OH group?

choices.text: On the top face of the ring
On the bottom face of the ring
choices.why: That is where the –CH2OH group goes in L sugars.

choices.text: It becomes part of the ring
choices.why: In glucose, the ring is closed by the carbon 5 –OH; the carbon 6 –CH2OH stays outside the ring.

choices.text: On either face, depending on whether the anomer is α or β
choices.why: The anomer is set at the anomeric carbon. The –CH2OH position depends on D or L.

explanation: For D sugars, the terminal –CH2OH group is on the top of the ring, whereas for L sugars, the –CH2OH group is on the bottom.

prompt: When a monosaccharide cyclizes, what is the anomeric center?

choices.text: The hemiacetal carbon, which was the carbonyl carbon
The carbon that supplies the ring oxygen (carbon 5 in glucose)
choices.why: That carbon keeps its configuration. The new chirality center forms at the former carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: The terminal –CH2OH carbon
choices.why: The –CH2OH carbon isn't a chirality center; the anomeric center is the hemiacetal carbon.

choices.text: The lowest chirality center, which decides D or L
choices.why: That center is unchanged on cyclization. The anomeric center is the new one at the former carbonyl carbon.

explanation: When an open-chain monosaccharide cyclizes to a pyranose form, a new chirality center is generated at the former carbonyl carbon, and two diastereomers called anomers are produced. The hemiacetal carbon atom is referred to as the anomeric center.

prompt: How does the section define the α anomer of D-glucopyranose?

choices.text: Its newly formed –OH at carbon 1 is cis to the –OH at the lowest chirality center in a Fischer projection
Its newly formed –OH at carbon 1 is trans to the –OH at the lowest chirality center in a Fischer projection
choices.why: That is the definition of the β anomer.

choices.text: Its –OH at carbon 1 is equatorial
choices.why: In α-D-glucopyranose the carbon 1 –OH is axial; it is equatorial in the β anomer.

choices.text: It is the anomer present in larger amount at equilibrium
choices.why: At equilibrium the mixture is 37 : 63 α : β, so the β anomer is the major one.

explanation: The anomer whose newly generated –OH group at carbon 1 is cis to the –OH at the lowest chirality center in a Fischer projection is the α anomer, α-D-glucopyranose. The one with that –OH trans is the β anomer, β-D-glucopyranose.

prompt: In aqueous solution, glucose cyclizes to an equilibrium mixture of α and β pyranose anomers. What percentage of that mixture is the β anomer?
explanation: Glucose cyclizes reversibly in aqueous solution to a 37 : 63 mixture of the α and β anomers, so the β anomer is 63%.

prompt: Why is β-D-glucopyranose the most stable of the eight D aldohexoses?

choices.text: Every ring substituent is equatorial, so it is the least crowded
Its anomeric –OH is axial, away from the other groups
choices.why: In β-D-glucopyranose the anomeric –OH is equatorial, like every other ring substituent.

choices.text: It is the only D aldohexose that can form a six-membered ring
choices.why: Other aldohexoses, such as mannose and galactose, also form pyranose rings.

choices.text: It has fewer chirality centers than the other D aldohexoses
choices.why: All aldohexose pyranoses have the same number of chirality centers; they differ in configuration.

explanation: In β-D-glucopyranose, all the substituents on the ring are equatorial. Thus, β-D-glucopyranose is the least sterically crowded and most stable of the eight D aldohexoses.

prompt: Which form of D-fructose is the most abundant in water solution?

choices.text: The β-pyranose
The β-furanose
choices.why: β-Furanose makes up 22.4%, second to the β-pyranose at 68%.

choices.text: The open-chain form
choices.why: Only 0.5% of D-fructose is open-chain in water.

choices.text: The α-pyranose
choices.why: α-Pyranose is just 2.7% of the mixture.

explanation: D-Fructose exists in water solution as 68% β-pyranose, 2.7% α-pyranose, 0.5% open-chain, 22.4% β-furanose, and 6.2% α-furanose.

prompt: In water solution, D-fructose is 22.4% β-furanose and 6.2% α-furanose. What total percentage of D-fructose is in a furanose form?
explanation: 22.4% + 6.2% = 28.6% furanose. The rest is mostly β-pyranose (68%), with 2.7% α-pyranose and 0.5% open-chain.

prompt: How do the pyranose and furanose forms of D-fructose arise?

choices.text: Pyranose: the carbon 6 –OH adds to the carbon 2 carbonyl; furanose: the carbon 5 –OH adds to the carbon 2 carbonyl
Pyranose: the carbon 5 –OH adds to the carbon 2 carbonyl; furanose: the carbon 6 –OH adds to the carbon 2 carbonyl
choices.why: That is reversed. The farther carbon 6 –OH gives the larger, six-membered pyranose ring.

choices.text: Pyranose: the carbon 5 –OH adds to the carbon 1 carbonyl; furanose: the carbon 4 –OH adds to the carbon 1 carbonyl
choices.why: Fructose is a ketose with its carbonyl at carbon 2, not carbon 1.

choices.text: Both arise from the carbon 6 –OH adding to the carbon 2 carbonyl
choices.why: One –OH can make only one ring size. The furanose comes from the carbon 5 –OH.

explanation: Fructose's carbonyl is at carbon 2. The pyranose form results from addition of the –OH at carbon 6 to the carbonyl group, while the furanose form results from addition of the –OH at carbon 5 (Figure 25.5.2).

prompt: Pure α-D-glucopyranose has [α]_D = +112.2, and pure β-D-glucopyranose has [α]_D = +18.7. When either is dissolved in water, its specific rotation slowly changes to what constant value?
explanation: Either anomer reaches the same constant value, +52.6: the α solution decreases from +112.2 to +52.6, and the β solution increases from +18.7 to +52.6. This change is called mutarotation.

prompt: What is mutarotation?

choices.text: The slow change in optical rotation as a pure anomer equilibrates with the other
The slow conversion of a D sugar into its L enantiomer in solution
choices.why: Mutarotation interconverts the α and β anomers of one sugar; the lowest chirality center isn't affected.

choices.text: The rapid flip of a pyranose ring between its two chair conformations
choices.why: A ring-flip doesn't break bonds. Mutarotation goes through ring-opening to the open-chain aldehyde.

choices.text: The change in a Fischer projection's meaning when it is rotated 90°
choices.why: That is about drawings, not a change in a real solution's optical rotation.

explanation: When a sample of either pure glucose anomer is dissolved in water, its optical rotation slowly changes until it reaches a constant value. This change, called mutarotation, is due to the slow interconversion of the pure anomers to give the same 37 : 63 equilibrium mixture.

prompt: How does mutarotation take place, and what speeds it up?

choices.text: Reversible ring-opening of each anomer to the open-chain aldehyde, then reclosure; catalyzed by both acid and base
Direct inversion at the anomeric carbon without ring-opening; catalyzed by light
choices.why: Mutarotation goes through ring-opening to the open-chain aldehyde, and acid and base catalyze it.

choices.text: Reversible ring-opening to the open-chain aldehyde, then reclosure; fast at neutral pH and slowed by acid
choices.why: The equilibration is slow at neutral pH and is catalyzed by both acid and base.

choices.text: A ring-flip between chair conformations; catalyzed by base only
choices.why: A ring-flip can't change the configuration at carbon 1. Ring-opening and reclosure do, catalyzed by acid and base.

explanation: Mutarotation occurs by a reversible ring-opening of each anomer to the open-chain aldehyde, followed by reclosure. Although the equilibration is slow at neutral pH, it is catalyzed by both acid and base.

prompt: In β-L-glucopyranose (Worked Example 25.5.2), which face of the ring holds the –CH2OH group and the anomeric –OH?

choices.text: Both are on the bottom face
Both are on the top face
choices.why: That is true of β-D-glucopyranose. The L enantiomer has every position reversed.

choices.text: The –CH2OH is on the top face and the anomeric –OH on the bottom face
choices.why: In an L sugar the –CH2OH is on the bottom face, and here the anomeric –OH is on the bottom too.

choices.text: The –CH2OH is on the bottom face and the anomeric –OH on the top face
choices.why: The worked example notes that the anomeric –OH is on the bottom face, along with the –CH2OH.

explanation: β-L-Glucopyranose is the mirror image of β-D-glucopyranose, so the stereochemistry at every ring position is changed. The –CH2OH group is on the bottom face of the ring in the L enantiomer, as is the anomeric –OH.

prompt: Ribose exists largely in a furanose form. Which –OH group adds to the carbon 1 aldehyde to form it?

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 4
The –OH at carbon 5
choices.why: Ring closure through the carbon 5 oxygen would give a six-membered pyranose ring.

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 3
choices.why: That would make a four-membered ring, which is strained. A furanose is five-membered.

choices.text: The –OH at carbon 2
choices.why: Carbon 2 is next to the aldehyde carbon; it can't close a five-membered ring.

explanation: A furanose is a five-membered cyclic hemiacetal. In Exercise 25.5.1, D-ribose's furanose form is produced by addition of the carbon 4 –OH group to the carbon 1 aldehyde, so the ring holds carbons 1 through 4 and one oxygen.

prompt: In their more stable chair conformations, which ring –OH group is axial in β-D-galactopyranose and in β-D-mannopyranose?

choices.text: The carbon 4 –OH in galactose; the carbon 2 –OH in mannose
The carbon 2 –OH in galactose; the carbon 4 –OH in mannose
choices.why: That is reversed. Mannose differs from glucose at carbon 2, galactose at carbon 4.

choices.text: The anomeric (carbon 1) –OH in both
choices.why: In these β anomers the anomeric –OH is equatorial.

choices.text: None in either; all their ring substituents are equatorial
choices.why: Only β-D-glucopyranose has every ring substituent equatorial. Each of these has one axial –OH.

explanation: β-D-Glucopyranose has all ring substituents equatorial. D-Mannose differs from D-glucose at carbon 2 and D-galactose at carbon 4, so in their β chairs the carbon 2 –OH of mannose and the carbon 4 –OH of galactose are axial (Exercise 25.5.3).

prompt: In the more stable chair conformation of β-L-galactopyranose, how many of the ring –OH groups are axial?
explanation: Exercise 25.5.4's answer shows β-L-galactopyranose with an axial –OH at carbon 4 and equatorial –OH groups at carbons 1, 2, and 3. Just one ring –OH is axial.
